'''Alfred Lewis Goldberg''' (September 3, 1942 – April 18, 2023) was an American [[Cell biology|cell biologist]]-[[biochemist]] and professor at [[Harvard University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cellbio.hms.harvard.edu/faculty-staff/alfred-goldberg|title=Alfred Goldberg|website=cellbio.hms.harvard.edu}}</ref> His major discoveries have concerned the mechanisms and physiological importance of [[protein degradation]] in cells.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://agoldberg.med.harvard.edu/|title=Home &#124; Goldberg Lab|website=agoldberg.med.harvard.edu}}</ref>

<!-- Of wide impact have been his lab's demonstration that all cells contain a pathway for selectively eliminating [[misfolded proteins]], his discoveries about the role of [[proteasomes]] in this process and of the enzyme systems catalyzing [[protein breakdown]] in [[bacteria]], his elucidating the mechanisms for [[muscle atrophy]] and the role of [[proteasomes]] in [[antigen presentation]] to the [[immune system]], and his introduction of proteasome inhibitors now widely used as research tools and in the treatment of [[blood cancers]]. ==Early life and career==
Goldberg was born in [[Providence, Rhode Island]] into a Jewish family on September 3, 1942, the son of Mr. and Mrs. Philip Goldberg. He graduated from [[Harvard College]] in 1963 ''[[magna cum laude]]'' in Biochemical Sciences (where he did his honor’s research in the laboratory of [[James Watson]]). He then spent a year as a Churchill Scholar at [[Cambridge University]], where he studied [[physiology]], before becoming a medical student at [[Harvard]]. After two years, he transferred to the Harvard Graduate School and in 1968 received his [[PhD]] in [[Physiology]] for studies in the laboratory of HM Goodman. He then joined the faculty at [[Harvard Medical School]] and rose to become full [[Professor]] of Physiology in 1977 and since 1993 Professor of Cell Biology. He also held visiting professorships at [[University of California (Berkeley)]] (1976), [[Institut Pasteur]] (Paris) (1995), and [[St John's College, Cambridge]] (2012).

==Research career==
In the 1960s, when Goldberg began his research career, there was little interest in protein degradation.<ref name="auto3">{{Cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2014.08.014 |title=Alfred Goldberg |date=2014 |last1=Goldberg |first1=Alfred |journal=Current Biology |volume=24 |issue=17 |pages=R780–R782 |pmid=25340212 |s2cid=20526006 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2014CBio...24.R780G }}</ref><ref name="auto2">{{cite journal|pmid=4604628 |date=1974 |last1=Goldberg |first1=A. L. |last2=Dice |first2=J. F. |title=Intracellular protein degradation in mammalian and bacterial cells |journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry |volume=43 |pages=835–869 |doi=10.1146/annurev.bi.43.070174.004155 }}</ref> However, as a graduate student, Goldberg showed that the loss of [[muscle mass]] upon [[denervation]] or [[fasting]] occurred primarily through acceleration of protein degradation.<ref name="auto">{{Cite journal |pmid=5792658 |date=1969 |last1=Goldberg |first1=A. L. |title=Protein turnover in skeletal muscle. II. Effects of denervation and cortisone on protein catabolism in skeletal muscle |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=244 |issue=12 |pages=3223–3229 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)93117-0 |doi-access=free }}</ref> As an assistant professor, he decided to focus on this neglected area,<ref name="auto3" /> and his early studies in [[E. coli]] and [[reticulocytes]] first demonstrated that cells rapidly degrade [[misfolded proteins]] as arise through [[mutations]] and errors in [[protein synthesis]].<ref>{{Cite journal |pmc=426471 |pmid=4551144 |date=1972 |last1=Goldberg |first1=A. L. |title=Degradation of abnormal proteins in Escherichia coli (Protein breakdown-protein structure-mistranslation-amino acid analogs-puromycin) |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=69 |issue=2 |pages=422–426 |doi=10.1073/pnas.69.2.422 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=14685250 |date=2003 |last1=Goldberg |first1=A. L. |title=Protein degradation and protection against misfolded or damaged proteins |journal=Nature |volume=426 |issue=6968 |pages=895–899 |doi=10.1038/nature02263 |bibcode=2003Natur.426..895G |s2cid=395463 }}</ref> These studies defined for the first time many of the key features of intracellular protein degradation,<ref name="auto2"/><ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=786161 |date=1976 |last1=Goldberg |first1=A. L. |last2=St John |first2=A. C. |title=Intracellular protein degradation in mammalian and bacterial cells: Part 2 |journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry |volume=45 |pages=747–803 |doi=10.1146/annurev.bi.45.070176.003531 }}</ref> especially its role in protein quality control in eliminating aggregation-prone proteins and its requirement for metabolic energy (ATP).<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=4565695 |date=1972 |last1=Prouty |first1=W. F. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=Fate of abnormal proteins in E. Coli accumulation in intracellular granules before catabolism |journal=Nature New Biology |volume=240 |issue=100 |pages=147–150 |doi=10.1038/newbio240147a0 }}</ref>

At that time, the [[lysosome]] was believed to be the only site for protein degradation in cells. However, in 1977, his lab demonstrated that the rapid breakdown of misfolded proteins in reticulocytes is catalyzed by a non-lysosomal, ATP-dependent system,<ref>{{Cite journal |pmc=393195 |pmid=264694 |date=1977 |last1=Etlinger |first1=J. D. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=A soluble ATP-dependent proteolytic system responsible for the degradation of abnormal proteins in reticulocytes |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=54–58 |doi=10.1073/pnas.74.1.54 |bibcode=1977PNAS...74...54E |doi-access=free }}</ref> now called the Ubiquitin Proteasome System. The seminal studies of [[Hershko]], [[Ciechanover]], and [[Rose|Irwin Rose]] on these preparations uncovered the role of ubiquitination in marking such proteins for degradation.<ref>{{Cite journal |doi=10.1146/annurev.biochem.67.1.425 |pmid=9759494 |title=The Ubiquitin System |date=1998 |last1=Hershko |first1=Avram |last2=Ciechanover |first2=Aaron |journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry |volume=67 |pages=425–479 }}</ref> Simultaneously, Goldberg and coworkers discovered that protein degradation in [[bacteria]], which lack [[ubiquitin]], and [[mitochondria]] involves a new type of [[enzyme]], [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]] hydrolyzing [[protease]] complexes ([[protease]] Lon/La, ClpAP, HslUV).<ref>{{Cite journal |pmc=320299 |pmid=6458037 |date=1981 |last1=Chung |first1=C. H. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=The product of the lon (CapR) gene in Escherichia coli is the ATP-dependent protease, protease la |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=78 |issue=8 |pages=4931–4935 |doi=10.1073/pnas.78.8.4931 |bibcode=1981PNAS...78.4931C |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=3303028 |date=1987 |last1=Hwang |first1=B. J. |last2=Park |first2=W. J. |last3=Chung |first3=C. H. |last4=Goldberg |first4=A. L. |title=Escherichia coli contains a soluble ATP-dependent protease (Ti) distinct from protease la |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=84 |issue=16 |pages=5550–5554 |doi=10.1073/pnas.84.16.5550 |pmc=298900 |bibcode=1987PNAS...84.5550H |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | pmc=346789 | date=1982 | last1=Waxman | first1=L. | last2=Goldberg | first2=A. L. | title=Protease la from Escherichia coli hydrolyzes ATP and proteins in a linked fashion | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume=79 | issue=16 | pages=4883–4887 | doi=10.1073/pnas.79.16.4883 | pmid=6214787 | bibcode=1982PNAS...79.4883W | doi-access=free }}</ref> They went on to describe their novel mechanisms<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=2938257 |date=1986 |last1=Waxman |first1=L. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=Selectivity of intracellular proteolysis: Protein substrates activate the ATP-dependent protease (La) |journal=Science |volume=232 |issue=4749 |pages=500–503 |doi=10.1126/science.2938257 |bibcode=1986Sci...232..500W }}</ref> and induction in stressful states.<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=3886165 |date=1985 |last1=Goff |first1=S. A. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=Production of abnormal proteins in E. Coli stimulates transcription of lon and other heat shock genes |journal=Cell |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=587–595 |doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(85)80031-3 |s2cid=205925149 }}</ref>

In 1987, his laboratory<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=3029081 |date=1987 |last1=Waxman |first1=L. |last2=Fagan |first2=J. M. |last3=Goldberg |first3=A. L. |title=Demonstration of two distinct high molecular weight proteases in rabbit reticulocytes, one of which degrades ubiquitin conjugates |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=262 |issue=6 |pages=2451–2457 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)61525-X |doi-access=free }}</ref> and Rechsteiner’s<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=3298229 |date=1987 |last1=Hough |first1=R. |last2=Pratt |first2=G. |last3=Rechsteiner |first3=M. |title=Purification of two high molecular weight proteases from rabbit reticulocyte lysate |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=262 |issue=17 |pages=8303–8313 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)47564-3 |doi-access=free }}</ref> described the much larger [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]]-dependent [[proteolytic]] complex that degrades ubiquitinated proteins in [[reticulocytes]]. He named it the [[26S proteasome]] to distinguish it from the smaller particle, which he named the [[20S proteasome]],<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=3277060 |date=1988 |last1=Arrigo |first1=A. P. |last2=Tanaka |first2=K. |last3=Goldberg |first3=A. L. |last4=Welch |first4=W. J. |title=Identity of the 19S 'prosome' particle with the large multifunctional protease complex of mammalian cells (The proteasome) |journal=Nature |volume=331 |issue=6152 |pages=192–194 |doi=10.1038/331192a0 |bibcode=1988Natur.331..192A |s2cid=97688 }}</ref> and which they later showed comprises the proteolytic activity of the 26S complex.<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=2180950 |date=1990 |last1=Driscoll |first1=J. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=The proteasome (Multicatalytic protease) is a component of the 1500-kDa proteolytic complex which degrades ubiquitin-conjugated proteins |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=265 |issue=9 |pages=4789–4792 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(19)34041-4 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Their subsequent studies defined many of the proteasome’s novel biochemical features, especially its ATP-dependent mechanism, peptide products, and cellular functions.<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=8811196 |date=1996 |last1=Coux |first1=O. |last2=Tanaka |first2=K. |last3=Goldberg |first3=A. L. |title=Structure and functions of the 20S and 26S proteasomes |journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry |volume=65 |pages=801–847 |doi=10.1146/annurev.bi.65.070196.004101 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |pmc=2083707 |date=2007 |last1=Smith |first1=D. M. |last2=Chang |first2=S. C. |last3=Park |first3=S. |last4=Finley |first4=D. |last5=Cheng |first5=Y. |last6=Goldberg |first6=A. |title=Docking of the Proteasomal ATPases' C-termini in the 20S Proteasomes alpha Ring Opens the Gate for Substrate Entry |journal=Molecular Cell |volume=27 |issue=5 |pages=731–744 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2007.06.033 |pmid=17803938 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |pmc=3063399 |date=2011 |last1=Smith |first1=D. L. |title=ATP binds to proteasomal ATPases in pairs with distinct functional effects implying an ordered reaction cycle |journal=Cell |volume=144 |issue=4 |pages=526–538 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.005 |pmid=21335235 }}</ref> Their recent research has shown that cellular rates of degradation are controlled in part by regulation of [[26S proteasome]] activity, including by [[protein kinases]].<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=26669444 |date=2015 |last1=Lokireddy |first1=S. |last2=Kukushkin |first2=N. L. |title=26S Proteasomes are rapidly activated by diverse hormones and physiological states that raise cAMP and cause Rpn6 phosphorylation |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=116 |issue=10 |pages=4228–4237 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1809254116 |pmc=6410790 |bibcode=2019PNAS..116.4228V |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=32513741 |date=2020 |author1=VerPlank JJS |last2=Tyrkalska |first2=S. Of major scientific and medical impact was his lab’s development of [[proteasome]] inhibitors that block degradation in cells.<ref name="auto5">{{Cite journal |pmid=8087844 |date=1994 |last1=Rock |first1=K. L. |last2=Gramm |first2=C. |last3=Rothstein |first3=L. |last4=Clark |first4=K. |last5=Stein |first5=R. |last6=Dick |first6=L. |last7=Hwang |first7=D. |last8=Goldberg |first8=A. L. |title=Inhibitors of the proteasome block the degradation of most cell proteins and the generation of peptides presented on MHC class I molecules |journal=Cell |volume=78 |issue=5 |pages=761–771 |doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(94)90462-6 |s2cid=22262916 }}</ref><ref name="auto4">{{Cite journal |pmc=3494858 |date=2012 |last1=Goldberg |first1=A. L. |title=Development of proteasome inhibitors as research tools and cancer drugs |journal=The Journal of Cell Biology |volume=199 |issue=4 |pages=583–588 |doi=10.1083/jcb.201210077 |pmid=23148232 }}</ref> In collaboration with a small biotech company (Myogenics/Proscript), which he founded, they introduced in 1994 the inhibitor, [[MG132]], which has been used in many thousands of publications and has enabled major advances in knowledge about the importance of protein degradation.<ref name="auto4" /><ref>{{Cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.tcb.2016.09.003 |title=Alfred L. Goldberg: Probing the Proteasome |journal=Trends in Cell Biology |date=2016 |volume=26 |issue=11 |pages=792–794 |pmid=27680754 }}</ref> In introducing these [[Enzyme inhibitor|inhibitor]]s,<ref name="auto5" /> they showed that the [[proteasome]] is the major site for [[protein breakdown]] in normal [[cell (biology)|cell]]s, is critical in activation of inflammatory responses,<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=8087845 |date=1994 |last1=Palombella |first1=V. J. |last2=Rando |first2=O. J. |last3=Goldberg |first3=A. L. |last4=Maniatis |first4=T. |title=The ubiquitin-proteasome pathway is required for processing the NF-kappa B1 precursor protein and the activation of NF-kappa B |journal=Cell |volume=78 |issue=5 |pages=773–785 |doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(94)90482-0 |s2cid=54245713 }}</ref> and is the source of most [[antigen]] peptides presented on surface MHC Class 1 molecules, which is critical in immune defense against [[viruses]] and [[cancer]]. His long collaboration with Ken Rock further elucidated this process,<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=10358773 |date=1999 |last1=Rock |first1=K. L. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=Degradation of cell proteins and the generation of MHC class I-presented peptides |journal=Annual Review of Immunology |volume=17 |pages=739–779 |doi=10.1146/annurev.immunol.17.1.739 }}</ref> identified the unique properties of the [[proteasomes]] in immune tissues,<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=8396732 |date=1993 |last1=Gaczynska |first1=M. |last2=Rock |first2=K. L. |last3=Goldberg |first3=A. L. |title=Gamma-interferon and expression of MHC genes regulate peptide hydrolysis by proteasomes |journal=Nature |volume=365 |issue=6443 |pages=264–267 |doi=10.1038/365264a0 |bibcode=1993Natur.365..264G |s2cid=4322260 }}</ref> and defined the roles of cellular peptidases (especially [[ERAP1]]) in further processing proteasome products so they fit into MHC Class 1 molecules.<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=12436109 |date=2002 |last1=Saric |first1=T. |last2=Chang |first2=S. C. |last3=Hattori |first3=A. |last4=York |first4=I. A. |last5=Markant |first5=S. |last6=Rock |first6=K. L. |last7=Tsujimoto |first7=M. |last8=Goldberg |first8=A. L. |title=An IFN-gamma-induced aminopeptidase in the ER, ERAP1, trims precursors to MHC class I-presented peptides |journal=Nature Immunology |volume=3 |issue=12 |pages=1169–1176 |doi=10.1038/ni859 |s2cid=21648629 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=12436110 |date=2002 |last1=York |first1=I. A. |last2=Chang |first2=S. C. |last3=Saric |first3=T. |last4=Keys |first4=J. A. |last5=Favreau |first5=J. M. |last6=Goldberg |first6=A. L. |last7=Rock |first7=K. L. |title=The ER aminopeptidase ERAP1 enhances or limits antigen presentation by trimming epitopes to 8-9 residues |journal=Nature Immunology |volume=3 |issue=12 |pages=1177–1184 |doi=10.1038/ni860 |s2cid=21337369 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Most importantly, Goldberg’s efforts initiated the development by the company of [[proteasome inhibitor]] [[Bortezomib]]/[[Velcade]], which is used worldwide to treat the common [[hematological cancer]], [[multiple myeloma]].<ref name="auto4" /> Over 600,000 patients have now been treated with proteasome inhibitors, which have extended their life spans and improved their quality of life.

Another area where the Goldberg lab has made major contributions concerns the cellular mechanisms of [[muscle atrophy]].<ref name="auto" /> His lab first identified factors that suppress [[muscle]] protein degradation (e.g., [[insulin]])<ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://www.jbc.org/article/S0021-9258(19)42013-9/pdf |pmid=1141208 |date=1975 |last1=Fulks |first1=R. L. |title=Effects of insulin, glucose, and amino acids on protein turnover in rat diaphragm |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=250 |issue=1 |pages=290–298 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(19)42013-9 |doi-access=free }}</ref> or enhance it (e.g., disuse, [[cancer cachexia]]),<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=8948566 |date=1996 |last1=Mitch |first1=W. E. |last2=Goldberg |first2=A. L. |title=Mechanisms of muscle wasting. The role of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=335 |issue=25 |pages=1897–2705 |doi=10.1056/NEJM199612193352507 }}</ref> and subsequently showed that various types of [[muscle wasting]] occur through [[transcription (biology)|transcription]] of a common set of atrophy-related genes (atrogenes).<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid=14718385 |date=2004 |last1=Lecker |first1=S. H. |last2=Jagoe |first2=R. T. |last3=Gilbert |first3=A. |last4=Gomes |first4=M. |last5=Baracos |first5=V. |last6=Bailey |first6=J. |last7=Price |first7=S. R. |last8=Mitch |first8=W. E. |last9=Goldberg |first9=A. L. |title=Multiple types of skeletal muscle atrophy involve a common program of changes in gene expression |journal=FASEB Journal |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=39–51 |doi=10.1096/fj.03-0610com |doi-access=free |s2cid=11659799 }}</ref> They also identified the critical [[transcription factor]] triggering this atrophy program (FoxO3)<ref>{{Cite journal |pmc=3619734 |date=2004 |last1=Sandri |first1=M. |last2=Sandri |first2=C. |last3=Gilbert |first3=A. |last4=Skurk |first4=C. |last5=Calabria |first5=E. |last6=Picard |first6=A. |last7=Walsh |first7=K. |last8=Schiaffino |first8=S. |last9=Lecker |first9=S. H. |last10=Goldberg |first10=A. A. |last3=Goldberg |first3=A. L. |title=Muscle wasting in disease: Molecular mechanisms and promising therapies |journal=Nature Reviews. Drug Discovery |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=58–74 |doi=10.1038/nrd4467 |s2cid=13957882 }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
In 1970, Goldberg married Joan Marilyn Helpern, a physician (hematologist).<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1970/05/25/archives/professor-weds-joan-m-helpern-medical-student.html Wedding announcement], nytimes.com. Accessed September 26, 2025.</ref> They had two children: [[Aaron Goldberg]], a well-known jazz pianist, and Julie B. Goldberg, a software engineer.{{citation needed|date=September 2025}}

Alfred L. Goldberg died on April 18, 2023, at the age of 80.<ref>{{cite web |title=Alfred L. "Fred" Goldberg |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/bostonglobe/name/alfred-goldberg-obituary?id=51669292 |website=Legacy |access-date=April 19, 2023}}</ref>
